What it is and why it matters: Where your agent builds and keeps your program. Pick the tool your team already works in. Note any second tool under What lives where.
If you use more than one tool, say what goes in each. E.g. policies, risk and vendor registers in Notion; other audit evidence collated in Drive.
What you want the agent to do for you. Manager runs it; Analyst prepares; Expert advises. Manager is recommended once you trust it to act.
Where you'll work with the agent day to day. Shapes how it reaches you, shares updates and collects what it needs.
How the agent should approach your compliance. Defaults reflect a lean, engineering-led model. Remove any that don't fit; add your own.
Who the agent reports to and asks for approval. Name, role and the best way to reach them.
How often the agent updates you. Covers progress, open questions and anything waiting on your approval.
The legal entity named on the report. Needed, with Domain, before AI drafts can run.
The website AI researches to draft the system description, commitments and boundaries.
Frameworks in scope, with SOC 2 by Trust Services Criteria. Each adds its own controls and evidence.
Type 1 tests design on a date. Type 2 tests operation over a period, so evidence must span it.
Type 2 review period as a range, or the Type 1 as-of date. Evidence must fall within it.
Link to the client's online terms of service. AI reads it for service commitments and SLAs.
Link to the client's online privacy policy. AI reads it for data handled and subprocessors.
Owns governance and business risk, often the CEO, CFO or COO. Name and title.
Owns systems and engineering, often the CTO, CISO, CPO or Head of Engineering. Name and title.
The person accountable for the compliance program, often the governance or technical lead.
Control owners and others involved: name, title and how they're involved, at a high level.
What the report covers and how it's delivered. Shapes system boundaries, controls and the responsibilities customers carry (CUECs).
Sets the audit window and readiness runway. Controls must be live, with evidence, before the period starts.
Scales onboarding, training, access reviews and offboarding controls. Also drives auditor sample sizes.
Calibrates how formal controls need to be. Lean and automated early; more defined ownership and cadence as you scale.
Where you operate and staff are based. Drives privacy, employment and data-transfer obligations, and where evidence is held.
Offices, data centres or fully remote. Physical sites add physical security controls; cloud-only teams rely on the provider's report.
Who you sell to sets the bar for assurance. Enterprise and regulated buyers expect stronger contracts, evidence and questionnaire answers.
Where customers are drives privacy laws, data residency and contract commitments.
The kinds of data your service holds. Sets confidentiality and privacy scope, how data is classified and which laws apply.
What you promise customers in contracts and SLAs. Paste the clauses or links; the agent pulls out the numbers and tests controls against them.
Laws and standards beyond SOC 2 that apply. Each adds obligations to map to controls and can widen scope (e.g. HIPAA, GDPR).
Vendors that deliver part of your service. Sets carve-out vs inclusive, the controls you rely on them for, and whose reports you review.
The rhythm leadership meets and aligns on. If it varies, pick the one to align around; reviews and sign-offs are built into it.
Roughly how often changes reach production. Pick the closest; N/A if you don't ship changes. Shapes change approval, evidence and samples.
Why you're doing this: deals, mandates, markets. Sets priorities and how effort is balanced between speed, rigour and customer assurance.
Where you are with compliance today. From just starting to audited before: sets where the agent focuses and how it helps.
Frameworks already in place or certified. Existing controls and evidence are reused, not rebuilt.
Frameworks you plan to add next. Controls are designed once and mapped across frameworks, so evidence serves every audit.
Weak spots you already know about. Past audit exceptions and open fixes: the agent tackles these before the auditor finds them.
Major changes expected in the next 12 months. New products, regions, tools, hires or funding. The agent adjusts scope ahead of time.
Whether an independent test is done or planned. Supports vulnerability management and is a top customer and auditor request.
How testing is done and by whom. Sets how much weight the results carry and how findings are tracked to closure.
The products and services the report covers. Anything not named here is out of scope. AI-drafted from the Domain; review before use.
Whether the product in scope is built and live. A Type 1 needs it live on the as-of date; until then the agent sets product controls for launch.
The cloud and network layer the product runs on. Anchors hardening, patching and network controls; evidence comes from cloud consoles and config.
Where the application is deployed and served. Defines shared responsibilities and a likely subservice organisation in the report.
Where customer data is stored. Drives encryption, backup and data access controls at the heart of the system boundary.
Email, documents and collaboration suite. Holds sensitive data too; sharing, MFA and admin settings are tested.
Platform that tracks controls and evidence. Sets how much evidence is automated and where the auditor looks first.
AI models and services in product or workplace. Adds AI governance, data-use and vendor controls; providers may be subservice organisations.
How data and systems are backed up and restored. Drives backup, restore testing and DR controls; evidence from backup logs and restore tests.
CDN, WAF and DDoS protection at the perimeter. Supports network security and availability; evidence from edge configuration and alerts.
The identity provider staff sign in with. Central to MFA, provisioning and offboarding; the main source for user lists and reviews.
How staff store and share credentials. Supports credential management controls; evidence from vault policies and settings.
Where keys, tokens and secrets are held. Drives encryption and key management controls; evidence from KMS or vault configuration.
How admin and production access is controlled. Shapes standing vs just-in-time access; evidence from approvals and session logs.
The tool that enrols and configures laptops. Enforces encryption, screen lock and updates; its reports are the device evidence.
Malware and threat protection on devices. Supports endpoint security controls; evidence from console coverage and alerts.
Where source code lives and is reviewed. Anchors change control: branch protection and pull request reviews are the core evidence.
How code is tested and released. Pipeline gates can replace manual approvals; deployment logs become change evidence.
How infrastructure is defined and changed. Infrastructure as code brings infra changes under review, with evidence in the repo.
Scans hosts, containers and cloud services. Drives vulnerability management and patch SLAs; evidence from scans and remediation tickets.
Scans code, dependencies and web apps. Supports secure development controls; evidence from scan results and fixes in PRs.
Continuous checks of cloud settings. Catches drift between reviews; findings and dashboards become automated evidence.
Where system and user activity is recorded. Underpins monitoring and investigations; coverage, retention and log access are tested.
Detects and alerts on suspicious activity. Drives monitoring and incident response; evidence from alerts and triage records.
Uptime, performance and error monitoring. Backs availability commitments and incident response; evidence from alerts and history.
Whether production scales automatically with load. Sets whether capacity is managed by configuration or by forecasting (Availability).
How customers hear about outages and maintenance. Evidence for availability commitments and incident communication.
Where joiners, movers and leavers are recorded. Drives account set-up and removal, and the population auditors sample.
Where requests, changes and incidents are tracked. The evidence trail for access requests, changes and incidents.
Where policies, procedures and runbooks live. The home for policy evidence, approvals and staff acknowledgements.
Tools that stop sensitive data leaving. Supports confidentiality controls; evidence from DLP policies and incidents.
Who operates the environment the service runs in. Sets which controls you own, which customers own (CUECs), and where the system boundary sits.
How customers are separated from each other. Drives segregation and data access controls, and how isolation is evidenced to customers.
How much sensitive data the service takes in. Less data means fewer privacy, retention and encryption controls to design and evidence.
Who decides where customer data is stored. Shapes residency commitments, encryption keys and the data-related CUECs.
How much customers rely on the service being up. Drives backup, DR, capacity and monitoring controls, and whether Availability is in scope.
How customers connect to the service. APIs and webhooks add key management, secure development and integration CUECs.
How central AI is to what customers receive. Adds AI governance, output monitoring and model provider controls as reliance grows.
Who administers customers' users and settings. Sets whether access CUECs apply or your own admin access controls carry the weight.
Who owns the results the service produces. Shapes commitments, processing integrity and how much customers must validate outputs.
How much the service varies per customer. Custom or managed elements add change and customer-specific controls to evidence.
When your people can see customer data. Drives support access, approval and logging controls, and confidentiality commitments.
Who grants and removes access to systems. Sets whether access evidence comes from one identity provider or from each system owner.
How changes are approved and reach production. Shapes change controls (CC8) and whether evidence lives in pipelines, pull requests or tickets.
How much of the stack you run yourselves. Managed services mean more reliance on provider reports and fewer hardening controls.
Where and how your people work. Shapes physical security, remote access and how onboarding and training are evidenced.
Who owns and manages the devices staff use. Managed devices are enforced and evidenced centrally; BYOD needs other safeguards.
How admin and production access is held. Standing access needs reviews and monitoring; JIT access is evidenced by requests and expiry.
How risks are identified and kept current. Sets assessment cadence and whether evidence is a periodic register or ongoing records.
Who selects and oversees vendors. Shapes vendor approval and review controls, and who holds the evidence.
Who leads when something goes wrong. Shapes incident roles, escalation and testing, and where incident records live.
How leadership oversees security and compliance. Sets whether oversight is evidenced by committee minutes or by everyday leadership forums.
Who or what performs routine controls. Automated and agent-run controls move evidence to system logs, with people handling exceptions.
